principles.text: Plan for both sides of the open: cover some shorts into an early dump (to free buying power for other shorts) or add shorts (DRAM names, SNDK) into a bounce.

A slow bleed (wide candles with gap downs, -15% in four sessions, no panic) tends to make a downtrend LONGER than a fast waterfall, which is better for short-term shorts; we haven't had a prolonged downtrend in years - most corrections have been fast flushes. QQQ still slightly below the 50 EMA, so wait to see how the market reacts.

Trickiest short pattern: what looks like a breakout of the prior-day high that gets rejected and closes below the anchored VWAP and 9 EMA near the low of day (MU) - the market 'confirming the weakness'. Between two candidates, short the weaker one.
Stay focused on the short side for the coming days unless the market proves otherwise; what would turn him long is the mirror image of what turned him short.
SPY hanging around the hourly 9 EMA is the tell: when SPY finds resistance at the hourly 9 EMA 'that's the time where the market really starts to tank.'

Doesn't juggle positions (closing working positions to free buying power) for a more aggressive, lower-win-rate entry like shorting SNDK at the lows; the best entries were higher up and he missed them.

Journaling now = entries and exits only; the daily pre-market writing (ideas for the day + reflection on the previous day) was dropped after ~1-1.5 years. No trading stats (win rate, avg win/loss) are useful to him, but journaling is 100% crucial because it is the first step to identifying and fixing mistakes - the big lessons are in the losing trades that traders in drawdown refuse to look at.

'1-minute breakout of the previous bar' in the first five minutes means the last 1-minute bar; later in the day it means the bar that touches the support/resistance level; a 5-minute bar is often better for the breakdown reference.

A short on the extension before price reaches the 21 EMA is fine if the stop is tight (~1.5%) and the entry is the first violation of a clean string of higher lows on the 5/15-minute chart; if stopped and it rallies into the 21, take another shot. You don't have to wait for the touch.
Trade what you see: whether RDDT is forming a late-stage VCP is irrelevant - it can gap 30% either way tomorrow.

Post-mortem on the TSLA stop-out: getting stopped when shorting at the lows means the entry was extended to the downside; next time wait for the bounce into the anchored VWAP / hourly EMAs. Pullbacks into resistance are the entry 'just because they work.'

Shorting a rejection of the declining 9 EMA while the 9 is still well above the 21 is a lower-win-rate, more aggressive short (LITE example); he prefers the 9 close to the 21, though an entry right at the high of day / declining 9 is great.

Ran out of buying power after the TSLA loss and watched SNDK and TSLA collapse without him: 'a man with a broken leg trying to shoot a penalty kick'; lesson - be more patient on entries so capital is available for the best one.
